DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# OPENING: Jesus had no biological father

**Position.** I defend the standard reading: Jesus had no human biological father. His conception in Mary was by the Holy Ghost, and Joseph was husband and legal guardian, not begetter.

**Term.** "Biological father" means the male parent who begets, the one the KJV marks with "begat." The Greek is *gennaō* (to beget, when said of a father; to bear or be born, when said of a mother). The question is whether the text assigns that act to a man.

---

## I. Matthew 1: the begetting chain breaks at Joseph

**1. The repeated "begat" stops.** [L1] Matthew 1:2-16 runs "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob…" through to verse 16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." [L2] Every "begat" is *egennēsen* (he begat), active voice, with a male subject. At verse 16 the pattern changes. The text says *ex hēs egennēthē Iēsous* (out of whom was born Jesus). *Hēs* (of whom) is feminine singular, so its antecedent can only be Mary, not Joseph. *Egennēthē* is passive (was born). Joseph is called *ton andra Marias* (the husband of Mary), and no active "begat" is ascribed to him. [L4] The genealogy has "begat" in every prior generation and withholds it here. Both the verb change (L2) and the feminine relative (L2) stand in the verse (L1). So the text deliberately declines to make Joseph the begetter.

**2. The source of the conception is stated.** [L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." [L2] *Prin ē sunelthein autous* (before they came together) uses *sunerchomai* (to come together), here marital union. *Heurethē en gastri echousa* means "was found having in womb." *Ek pneumatos hagiou* means "out of Spirit holy," and *ek* (out of) marks source or origin. [L1] Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." [L2] *To gennēthen en autē* (that which has been begotten or conceived in her) is the same *gennaō*, and *ek pneumatos estin hagiou* gives its source as the Holy Ghost. [L4] The word that elsewhere names a father's begetting is used here, and its source is *ek pneumatos* (out of Spirit). That leaves no place for a human male source.

**3. Joseph's own reaction fits no other reading.** [L1] Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." [L2] *Apolusai* (to dismiss, to release) is the word for divorce. [L1] Matthew 1:20 then has the angel say "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife." [L4] Joseph knew he was not the father (Matt 1:19), and he accepted the pregnancy only after the angel's word (Matt 1:20). The reassurance would be needless if he were the father.

**4. No union before the birth.** [L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." [L2] *Ouk eginōsken* (he was not knowing) uses *ginōskō* (to know), the verb for marital intimacy. [L3] Genesis 4:1, "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived," uses *yada'* (to know) in the same sense. This verse speaks only of the time up to the birth, and that is all my case needs. [L4] Both the verb's idiom (L2, Gen 4:1) and Matthew's statement (L1) place the conception wholly outside any union with Joseph.

## II. Luke 1: Mary's own statement and the angel's answer

**5.** [L1] Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" [L2] *Andra ou ginōskō* (a man I do not know) has *ginōskō* in the present tense, a current condition. [L1] Luke 1:35 answers: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." [L2] *Epeleusetai* (shall come upon) and *episkiasei* (shall overshadow) are the promised agency. *Gennōmenon ek sou* (being born out of you) names Mary as the only human source. [L4] Mary asks how it can happen without a man, and the angel answers by naming a divine agency instead of a man (Luke 1:35). So the reply confirms that no man is involved.

**6. The "father" language is accounted for.** [L1] Luke 3:23: "Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." [L2] *Enomizeto* (was supposed, was reckoned by custom) marks a belief, not a fact. [L1] John 6:42, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?", is what the crowd says, not the narrator. [L1] Luke 2:48 has Mary say "thy father and I have sought thee," and Luke 2:49 corrects the word: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" [L4] Luke 3:23 itself says "as was supposed," so every verse calling Joseph the father reports appearance. Luke 2:48-49 then shows the correction in the same passage.

## III. The prophetic footing

**7.** [L1] Matthew 1:22-23 cites Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son." [L2] The Hebrew is *'almah* (a young woman of marriageable age). Matthew's Greek is *parthenos* (virgin). [L3] *'Almah* is used of Rebekah in Genesis 24:43, and Genesis 24:16 describes the same woman with *bethulah* (virgin) and says "neither had any man known her." So *'almah* can describe a woman who has not known a man. Matthew's inspired choice of *parthenos* (Matt 1:23), together with Matthew 1:18-25, fixes the sense for this sign. [L3] Genesis 3:15 speaks of "her seed," *zera'* (seed). That word is ordinarily reckoned through the male, and here it is reckoned through the woman. [L3] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman" (*genomenon ek gynaikos*, coming to be out of a woman), names only a woman. [L4] A sign given to the house of David (Isa 7:13-14) concerns a conception unlike an ordinary one. Matthew's *parthenos* (L2) and the other scriptures that trace the seed to the woman alone (L3) confirm that the sign is a conception without a man.

## IV. Anticipated objections

- **"Joseph is in the genealogy, so he is the father."** [L1] Matthew 1:16 does not say Joseph begat Jesus. It says Joseph is "husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus." [L3] Joseph's line gives the legal right to David's throne, because he took Mary as wife (Matt 1:20, 24) and named the child (Matt 1:25). [L3] Romans 1:3, "made of the seed of David according to the flesh," shows the fleshly descent also ran through Mary, since Joseph was not the begetter.
- **"Matthew 1:25 says 'till.'"** [L1] The verse limits only what happened before the birth, which is the point at issue.
- **"Spirit-conception is not 'biological.'"** [L1] Luke 1:35 says "that which shall be born of thee." Mary's flesh is the human source, as Galatians 4:4 says "of a woman," and no man's seed is named anywhere in the narrative.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" pattern: [L1] Matt 1:2-16 has *egennēsen* (he begat) in each prior generation; [L2] verse 16 uses feminine singular *hēs* (of whom) with passive *egennēthē* (was born) and calls Joseph only *andra* (husband), so Joseph is not named as begetter.
2. Matthew states the source of the conception as the Holy Ghost: [L1] Matt 1:18, 20 "of the Holy Ghost"; [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of Spirit holy) uses *ek* (out of, source) with *gennaō* (to beget or conceive); [L3] Luke 1:35 names the same agency.
3. Mary and Joseph both treat the pregnancy as without a man: [L1] Luke 1:34 "I know not a man" and Matt 1:19-20, 25; [L2] *ginōskō* (to know) as the marital idiom, matched at [L3] Gen 4:1 *yada'* (to know).
4. Every "father" reference to Joseph is reported supposition, not fact: [L1] Luke 3:23 "as was supposed"; [L2] *enomizeto* (was supposed, reckoned by custom); [L3] Luke 2:48-49 corrected by "my Father's business," and John 6:42 as the crowd's words.
5. The prophetic pattern places the seed in the woman alone: [L1] Matt 1:23 quoting Isa 7:14 "a virgin"; [L2] *'almah* (young woman of marriageable age) rendered *parthenos* (virgin); [L3] Gen 24:16, 43 for the *'almah*/virgin usage, Gen 3:15 "her seed," and Gal 4:4 "made of a woman."
6. Therefore Jesus had no human biological father: [L1] Matt 1:18-20, Luke 1:34-35; [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of Spirit holy) and *ek hēs* (out of whom, feminine); [L3] Gal 4:4 and Gen 3:15. His conception came by the Holy Ghost in Mary, and Joseph was husband and legal guardian, not begetter.

# CHALLENGER OPENING — the seed is out of a man's body, and the man is named

The question is whether the text assigns the begetting to a man. It does — in the promise's own words, in the naming, and in the reckoning. I press the keystone **D6** first, then the links it stands on.

---

## TARGET D6 and D5 — the promised seed is out of the loins; "of a woman" names mortality, not the absence of a father

[L1] "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12) — the throne-seed comes out of a man's body. [L1] "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne" (Psalm 132:11). [L1] "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne" (Acts 2:30). [L2] *osphys* (the loins) is the same word Hebrews 7:5, 10 uses for Levi "in the loins of his father." [L1] "made of the seed of David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3); [L2] *kata sarka* (according to flesh) is the biological marker — and it is precisely what Matthew 1:20 does **not** carry. [L1] "it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda" (Hebrews 7:14) — [L2] *anatellō* (sprang up) — and the tribe is counted "by the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:2, 18). [L1] "Jesus Christ of the seed of David" (2 Timothy 2:8).

A legal guardian produces no seed: the seed must "proceed out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12). If Joseph begets nothing, D6 leaves the promise of the flesh-seed with **no row anywhere in the narrative**.

**D5's "made of a woman" is the mortality idiom, and the text itself supplies the check.** [L1] "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman" (Galatians 4:4) — the same phrase is said of John: "among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist" (Matthew 11:11), and the same gospel names his father, Zacharias (Luke 1:13, 57). [L3] Job 14:1 "man that is born of a woman is of few days"; Job 15:14 "he which is born of a woman"; Job 25:4 "how can he be clean that is born of a woman?" [L4] "Born of a woman" marks frailty and mortality; it does not exclude a father — John is the proof-case. Footing: [L1] Matthew 11:11 with Luke 1:13 + [L3] the three Job rows.

**D5's "seed in the woman alone" is one row, and it is not Davidic.** [L1] Genesis 3:15 "her seed" (*zera'*, offspring). [L3] The offspring rows that predicate seed of a woman are four — Genesis 3:15, 16:10 (Hagar), 24:60 (Rebekah), Isaiah 54:3 (Zion) — none of them Davidic, and none of them a statement of how a child is begotten.

**The flesh D5 routes through Mary is not in the text.** Mary is given no lineage. [L1] Luke 1:36 names her kinswoman (*syngenēs*, of kin) Elisabeth, who is "of the daughters of Aaron" (Luke 1:5) — a priestly house, not David's. The only Davidic line named is Joseph's: "of the house of David" (Luke 1:27), "of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4), and the throne "of his father David" (Luke 1:32). "Mary's genealogy" is an import; the text never writes one.

---

## TARGET D1 — the passive verb is non-narration, and the register runs by the father's house

[L1] "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ" (Matthew 1:16). [L2] *egennēthē* (was born) is passive; *hēs* (of whom) is feminine. [L4] A silent passive does not say Joseph did not beget; it does not narrate the begetting, and one un-narrating verb cannot overrule the rows that name the father and the loins. Footing: [L1] the naming rows and the seed rows + [L2] the passive's own silence.

The register is not neutral: the line is Joseph's ("Jacob begat Joseph"), and the reckoning rule is the father's house — "by the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:2, 18); he who could not show it was put out (Ezra 2:59, margin "or, pedigree"); the priests called after the **wife's** house were "as polluted, put from the priesthood" (Ezra 2:61-62). [L1/L3] D1's "legal right through the wife" reading walks straight into the canon's own rule against it. And the father's act is narrated: "thou shalt call his name JESUS" (Matthew 1:21), "he called his name JESUS" (1:25) — the naming is the father's (Luke 1:13; 1:62-63).

---

## TARGET D2 — "of the Holy Ghost" is covenant origin; the two verbs are power and presence

[L1] "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:20). [L2] *ek* (out of) with God or the Spirit is the covenant-origin marker: "born of God" (John 1:13; 1 John 3:9; 5:1), "is of God" (1 John 4:7) — spiritual origin at every row, never biological paternity. Where the text means flesh it says so: *kata sarka*, Romans 1:3.

[L1] "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee" (Luke 1:35). [L2] *eperchomai* (come upon) is anointing and power — "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you, and ye shall be witnesses" (Acts 1:8), said of the apostles. *episkiazō* (overshadow) is the presence cloud — the transfiguration cloud (Matthew 17:5; Luke 9:34) and Peter's shadow (Acts 5:15). [L3] Neither verb denotes begetting at any row. And the title is *given*, not begotten: "shall be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35) — the covenant title God gave Solomon while Solomon had a father: "Solomon thy son... I have chosen him to be my son" (1 Chronicles 28:6). D2's "agency" is no begetting row.

---

## TARGET D3 — the timing rows bound the abstinence; the espousal was a marriage

[L1] "seeing I know not a man" (Luke 1:34). [L2] *andra ou ginōskō* (a man I do not know) is present active indicative: her state when the angel spoke, not a vow. [L1] "before they came together, she was found with child" (Matthew 1:18) dates the **finding**; [L2] *synerchomai* (come together) names married union elsewhere ("come together again," 1 Corinthians 7:5), and Matthew says what the coming together is: "took unto him his wife" (1:24). [L1] "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" (1:25) — [L2] *ouk eginōsken* (he was not knowing): the abstinence covers the pregnancy and is bounded by "till." [L3] And the canon's stated means of begetting is that knowing: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1).

They were husband and wife in law from the espousal: "Joseph her husband" (Matthew 1:19); "Mary thy wife" (1:20); the law calls a betrothed damsel "his neighbour's wife" (Deuteronomy 22:24). [L4] **Therefore the child of Mary, wife of Joseph of the house of David, is of his loins within the espousal.** Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:19, 20, 25 + [L3] Genesis 4:1 + [L2] the till-bounded imperfect of *ginōskō*.

---

## TARGET D4 — the father is named in four registers; "as was supposed" carries no verdict

[L1] Mary's own mouth, after the angel's words (Luke 1:26-38): "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48). [L1] The narrator: "the parents brought in the child Jesus" (2:27), "his parents went to Jerusalem" (2:41), "Joseph and his mother marvelled" (2:33). [L1] The town: "Is not this Joseph's son?" (Luke 4:22). [L1] A disciple: "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45). [L1] The angel: "Joseph, thou son of David" (Matthew 1:20).

[L2] *enomizeto* (was supposed, was wont) is the verb of "where prayer was wont to be made" (Acts 16:13) and "supposing him to have been in the company" (Luke 2:44) — custom and reckoning, no verdict of its own. Luke 2:49 "my Father's business" answers the child's mission; the same narrator still says "Joseph and his mother" (2:33). The two registers stand in one passage and the text resolves neither — a father in the house and a Father in the covenant title (1 Chronicles 28:6).

# DEFENDER, ROUND 2

The challenger has attacked six links one at a time. The case is the chain, so I re-seat each term in its chain and do not argue any term alone. Where the challenger's reading of a verse is accurate in isolation, the response is: **Noted. Not conceding here. Goes to review.**

---

## A. THE KEYSTONE (D6): the throne-seed and the man's loins

**A1. The seed texts cannot run through Joseph's body.**
[L1] Jeremiah 22:30: "Write ye this man childless… for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David." [L2] *zera'* (seed) is the word the text uses, and *'ariri* (childless, stripped) is the sentence on Coniah. [L1] Matthew 1:11-12 places Jechonias in Joseph's line, and Matthew 1:16 has "Jacob begat Joseph." [L4] If Joseph begat Jesus, then Jesus is of Jechonias's seed (Matt 1:12, 16), and Jeremiah 22:30 bars that seed from the throne. Matthew gives Joseph's line but withholds "begat" at its last link (Matt 1:16). The text itself therefore keeps the throne-right and the barred seed apart. This rests on [L1] Jer 22:30 + [L1] Matt 1:11-16 + [L2] *zera'* and the verb of verse 16.

**A2. In the Davidic promise the Father is named, and he is God.**
[L1] 2 Samuel 7:12 says "thy seed… out of thy bowels." Verse 14, the same promise, says "I will be his father, and he shall be my son." [L3] Hebrews 1:5 quotes 2 Samuel 7:14 of the one "better than the angels": "I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son." [L1] Luke 1:32, 35 joins "the throne of his father David" to "the Son of the Highest" and "the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee." [L4] The father assigned in the throne-promise itself is God (2 Sam 7:14; Heb 1:5), and Luke 1:35 places the Highest in the conception. The challenger cites 2 Samuel 7:12 but passes over verse 14 in the same promise.

**A3. "Loins" and "fruit of the loins" mark descent across generations, not the immediate begetter.**
[L1] Hebrews 7:10: Levi "was yet in the loins of his father [Abraham]," four generations before. [L3] Genesis 35:11: "kings shall come out of thy loins." Genesis 46:26 speaks of "all the souls that came with Jacob into Egypt, which came out of his loins." [L2] *osphys* (loins) in Acts 2:30 and Hebrews 7:5, 10 therefore reckons David's descendants. It does not require that no woman stands between David and the child. [L1] Hebrews 7:14, "sprang out of Juda" (*anatetalken*, has risen up), names a tribe and says nothing of the immediate begetter.

**A4. "According to the flesh" is satisfied by the woman.**
[L1] Romans 1:3 says "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." [L2] *genomenou* (coming to be, being made) is the same participle family as Galatians 4:4, *genomenon ek gynaikos* (coming to be out of a woman). [L3] Hebrews 2:14, 16: "he also himself likewise took part of the same [flesh and blood]… he took on him the seed of Abraham." [L2] *metesche* (partook) and *epilambanetai* (takes hold of) speak of a taking-on of flesh and say nothing of a human father's act. [L4] "Flesh" in Romans 1:3 means real human nature of David's line (Heb 2:14, 16), and it is said of the one "made," not of a begetter.

**A5. Mary's line is in the text.**
[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli." Matthew 1:16 gives Joseph's father as Jacob. [L2] Luke 3 has only *tou* (of the), with no *egennēsen* (he begat). [L1] Luke 3:31 names "Nathan, which was the son of David," a different son of David from Solomon (cf. Matt 1:6). [L4] Two lists, two fathers for Joseph, and Luke's parenthesis "(as was supposed)" placed at the very point where sonship to Joseph is named. These footings point to Luke giving the line through Mary, with Heli as her father, and Joseph entering as husband. I rest on [L1] Luke 3:23-31 + Matt 1:16 + [L2] the bare genitive. I do not rest the keystone on this alone, since A1–A4 and A2 stand independently.

**A6. The Aaronic kinswoman does not displace this.**
[L1] Luke 1:36, 5 makes Elisabeth of Aaron's daughters. [L1] Exodus 6:23: Aaron "took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab"; [L1] Numbers 1:7 makes Nahshon son of Amminadab "prince of the children of Judah." [L3] Priest and Judah intermarried at the root. Kinship in Luke 1:36 therefore does not cut Mary off from Judah.

---

## B. D5: "of a woman" and the seed texts

[L4] I do not rest the case on Galatians 4:4 alone, and the challenger's Job rows are noted and not conceded as isolated idiom. The chain matters here:

[L1] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." [L2] *exapesteilen* (sent forth) comes before *genomenon* (being made), so the one sent is a Son before he is made. [L1] John is "born of women" (Matt 11:11) and the text names his father (Luke 1:13, 57). Jesus is "conceived… of the Holy Ghost" (Matt 1:20), and the text names no father. [L4] The idiom does not carry the claim alone, and I do not need it to. The claim stands on Matthew 1:18-20 and Luke 1:35, and Galatians 4:4 is consistent with it. The contrast between the two cases lies in what the two narratives themselves state: John's father is named in the annunciation (Luke 1:13), and Jesus's father is named as God (Luke 1:32, 35).

---

## C. D1: the passive verb, the register, and the naming

**C1. The evangelist announces that the genealogy is not the account of the begetting.**
[L1] Matthew 1:1: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ." [L1] Matthew 1:18: "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise." [L2] *geneseōs* (of generation) in verse 1 and *gennēsis* (birth, coming to be) in verse 18 are the same root. *Houtōs* (thus, in this manner) introduces a manner distinct from the begetting chain just given. [L4] The chain ends at verse 16 with a woman as the antecedent. Verse 18 then says how the birth came about, and gives the Holy Ghost (v. 18, 20). So the passive at verse 16 is part of an announced shift of manner. It is not a stray silence. [L4] A formula repeated through the generations and altered at its last member is a datum.

**C2. The canon reckons through a woman at the roots.**
The challenger says the canon's own rule runs against the wife's house.
[L1] Ezra 2:61 itself reports a man who "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai… and was called after their name." [L1] 1 Chronicles 2:34-35: Sheshan "gave his daughter to Jarha his servant to wife; and she bare him Attai," and the line is carried on. [L1] 1 Chronicles 2:21-22 reckons Jair through Hezron's daughter, and Numbers 32:41 says "Jair the son of Manasseh." [L1] Numbers 27:1-7 and 36:6-8 treat daughters as carrying a father's inheritance. [L4] The register has precedent for reckoning through the woman, and the challenger's "rule against" overstates it (Ezra 2:61; 1 Chr 2:21-22, 34-35; Num 27, 32:41).

**C3. The naming is not the father's act only.**
[L1] Luke 1:31 says to Mary, "thou shalt call his name JESUS." [L1] Matthew 1:21 says the same to Joseph. [L1] Genesis 29:32 has Leah calling Reuben's name, and Luke 1:60 has Elisabeth giving John's name. [L1] Isaiah 7:14 says "she shall call his name Immanuel." [L4] Naming is attested of the mother as well as the father, so it does not establish a begetting row.

---

## D. D2: "of the Holy Ghost" and the two verbs

**D1. *Ek* (out of) is read in its sentence.**
[L1] John 1:13 is about believers: "which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
